stimuli.title: Waiting for an Answer
stimuli.text:
In most classrooms, a teacher who asks a question waits about one second before calling on a student or answering it herself. Researchers who timed these pauses in the 1970s were surprised by how short they were, and even more surprised by what happened when teachers were coached to stretch them to three seconds or more.

With longer pauses, students gave longer answers. More students volunteered, including some who rarely spoke. Answers were more likely to include a reason or an example, and students began responding to one another instead of only to the teacher. The questions themselves did not change; only the silence after them did.

Why should a few seconds matter so much? A question that asks students to explain or compare takes time to think through. When the teacher moves on after a single beat, the only students who can keep up are the ones who already knew the answer, and everyone else learns that it is safe to wait to be rescued.

Extending wait time is harder than it sounds. Three seconds of classroom silence can feel endless, and many teachers fill it out of habit. Some count silently; others tell the class in advance that no one will be called on until everyone has had time to think.

Wait time is not a cure for every problem. It does little for a question that has a one-word answer, and it cannot replace a well-planned lesson. But few changes cost so little, and few are so easy to try tomorrow morning.

stimuli.title: The Monarch's Long Road
stimuli.text:
Each fall, monarch butterflies from eastern North America fly as far as 3,000 miles to a few mountain forests in central Mexico. No single butterfly makes the round trip. The monarchs that fly south in autumn spend the winter clustered on fir trees, then start north in spring. They lay eggs on milkweed in the southern United States and die. Their offspring continue north, and it takes several generations to reach Canada by summer. The generation born at the end of summer is different: it delays breeding, stores fat and makes the whole journey south.

Because monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, the butterflies depend on that plant along the entire route. Where milkweed is cleared from roadsides and fields, fewer caterpillars survive to continue the journey.

stimuli.title: A Letter Home
stimuli.text:
Dear Families,

Beginning Monday, March 2, Lincoln Elementary will open its doors at 7:45 a.m. instead of 8:00 a.m. Breakfast will be served in the cafeteria from 7:45 to 8:10, and classes will start at 8:15 as they do now.

We are making this change because many of you told us in our winter survey that the 8:00 opening did not fit your work schedules. Opening earlier also gives every student who wants breakfast enough time to eat before class. However, the front office will still open at 8:00, so please call after that time to report an absence.

Thank you for your patience as we adjust. If you have questions, please contact the office.

Sincerely,

Ms. Ortega, Principal

stimuli.title: Two Views on Homework in the Early Grades
stimuli.text:
**Passage A**

Homework in kindergarten through second grade should be limited to reading with a family member. Young children gain little from worksheets at the kitchen table, and long assignments mostly teach them to dislike school. Twenty minutes with a book does more good than an hour of drills.

**Passage B**

A small amount of practice at home helps young students remember what they learned that day. Five or ten minutes of math facts or spelling words also shows parents what their child is studying. The key is to keep assignments short; the goal is a habit, not a burden.

stimuli.title: Spacing It Out
stimuli.text:
Most students study the way they were taught to: in one long session the night before a test. The habit makes sense on the surface. The material is fresh, and by the end of the evening it feels familiar. But feeling familiar with something is not the same as being able to recall it a week later.

A large body of memory research points to a different approach. When the same amount of study time is divided into shorter sessions spread over several days, people remember far more of it later. The effect, called spacing, has been found with vocabulary, history facts, math procedures and even motor skills.

One explanation is that a little forgetting helps. When a student returns to a topic after a gap, she has to work to bring it back to mind, and that effort strengthens the memory. Cramming skips the effort, because nothing has had time to fade.

Spacing has a cost: it feels harder. Students who space their study often believe, wrongly, that they are learning less, simply because each session involves more struggle. Teachers can help by building review of older material into homework and quizzes, so that spacing happens without anyone having to choose it.

None of this means that a review the night before a test is useless. It means that the night before should be the last of several sessions, not the only one.

stimuli.title: The Dust Bowl
stimuli.text:
In the 1920s, farmers on the southern Great Plains plowed up millions of acres of native grassland to plant wheat. Prices were high and rain was plentiful, so the gamble paid. Then, in the early 1930s, a long drought set in. With the deep-rooted grasses gone, nothing held the dry soil in place. Strong winds lifted it into enormous clouds of dust, some of which drifted as far as the Atlantic coast.

Thousands of families lost their farms and moved west in search of work. In response, the federal government created the Soil Conservation Service in 1935. It paid farmers to adopt methods such as planting rows of trees as windbreaks and plowing along the curves of the land rather than in straight lines.

stimuli.title: Notice to Residents of Maple Avenue
stimuli.text:
The City Water Department will replace the water main under Maple Avenue between 3rd and 6th Streets.

Work will begin on June 8. First, crews will mark the location of existing pipes and lines. Next, they will dig a trench and install the new main one block at a time. Finally, each home will be connected to the new main and the street will be repaved.

During connection work, water service to each home will be shut off for up to four hours. Residents will receive a door notice at least 48 hours before their service is interrupted. Street parking will not be available on the block where crews are working. The project is expected to be finished by the end of August, weather permitting.

Questions may be directed to the Water Department's project line.

stimuli.title: Two Views on Year-Round School Calendars
stimuli.text:
**Passage A**

A year-round calendar replaces the long summer break with several shorter breaks. Students forget less over a three-week break than over a ten-week one, so teachers spend less of each fall reteaching last year's lessons.

**Passage B**

Studies of year-round calendars have found only small differences in achievement, and the differences are not consistent from one district to the next. Meanwhile, families with children in different schools can end up with vacations that never line up.

stimuli.title: Hunting in the Dark
stimuli.text:
A barn owl can catch a mouse in complete darkness. For years, scientists assumed the owl must see better in the dark than other birds, and its eyes are indeed sensitive. But experiments in rooms with no light at all showed that the owl's hearing does most of the work.

The owl's face is shaped like a shallow dish of stiff feathers that collects sound and funnels it toward the ears. The ears themselves are set at slightly different heights on the head, so a rustle below the bird reaches one ear a tiny fraction of a second before the other. From that difference the owl judges not only the direction of a sound but also how far below it the source lies.

The owl's wing feathers have soft, comb-like edges that muffle the noise of flight. As a result, the owl can hear its prey while flying, and the prey cannot hear the owl coming.

stimuli.title: Opinion: Let's Keep Teaching Cursive
stimuli.text:
Some schools have dropped cursive handwriting to make room for keyboarding. That is a shortsighted trade.

Every student needs to type, but typing can be learned quickly at almost any age. Cursive, on the other hand, is rarely picked up later if it is not taught in school. A student who never learns it cannot read a grandparent's letters or many of the historical documents kept in archives.

Supporters of keyboarding point out that adults seldom write by hand at work. True enough. But we do not teach children only the skills they will use at a job. We teach them to read music, to draw maps and to recite poems, because these things connect them to the world around them. Surely an hour a week for cursive is a small price to pay. Any school board that cares about its students will restore it.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Longer pauses after questions help students
Students should answer only when they are called on
Teachers ask too many questions in class
Research from the 1970s is out of date
questions.explanation: The passage reports what happened when pauses grew to three seconds and ends by urging teachers to try it. The other choices are either not claimed or contradicted.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which change was observed when teachers waited longer?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says students began responding to one another instead of only to the teacher. It also says the questions themselves did not change.

questions.stem: In the third paragraph, the phrase "wait to be rescued" most nearly means:
options: wait for help from a classmate
wait for the bell to end class
wait for the answer to be given
wait for the lesson to be repeated
questions.explanation: The paragraph says that when the teacher moves on quickly, students who did not know the answer learn they can simply wait; someone else will supply it.

questions.stem: Which word best describes the author's attitude toward extending wait time?
questions.explanation: The author recommends trying it ("few changes cost so little") but also admits its limits ("not a cure for every problem"), so the support is tempered, not uncritical.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument?
options: Scores rose in classes that used longer pauses
Wait time was first studied in science classes
Students like questions with one-word answers
questions.explanation: The author argues that a longer pause improves learning. Evidence that results improved where pauses were longer supports that claim; teacher preference and the history of the research do not.

questions.stem: The author's explanation in the third paragraph assumes that:
options: teachers want students to stay silent
thinking through a hard question takes time
most students already know the answers
one-word questions teach students the most
questions.explanation: The paragraph says questions that ask students to explain or compare take time to think through, so a one-beat pause leaves most students behind. That reasoning depends on thinking taking time.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens right after the wintering monarchs start north in spring?
options: They store fat for the trip south
They lay eggs on milkweed and die
questions.explanation: The passage says the monarchs start north, lay eggs on milkweed in the southern United States and die; their offspring continue the trip.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the monarchs reaching Canada in summer:
options: make the trip south that same year
were born in the previous fall
questions.explanation: It takes several generations to reach Canada, so the summer arrivals are descendants of the butterflies that wintered in Mexico, not the same individuals.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, what would most likely happen if milkweed were removed along much of the route?
options: Fewer monarchs would complete the journey
Monarchs would stop flying south to Mexico
Monarchs would switch to fir trees
questions.explanation: Caterpillars eat only milkweed, and the passage says fewer survive where it is cleared. Less milkweed would mean fewer butterflies continuing the migration.

questions.stem: Which additional fact would be most relevant to the point made in the second paragraph?
options: How fast a monarch beats its wings
How much milkweed grows along the route
How many colors a monarch's wings can show
How long the fir trees in Mexico live
questions.explanation: The second paragraph is about the monarchs' dependence on milkweed along the route. Information on how much milkweed is available bears directly on that point.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the letter?
options: To change the time that classes begin
To report the winter survey results
To announce an earlier opening time
To ask families to report absences
questions.explanation: The letter tells families the doors will open at 7:45 starting March 2. Class start time stays at 8:15, and the survey is mentioned only as the reason.

questions.stem: According to the letter, when should a family call to report an absence?
questions.explanation: The letter says the front office will still open at 8:00, so families should call after that time.

questions.stem: In the paragraph that begins "We are making this change," the word "However" signals that the next sentence:
options: states the result of the change
gives an example of the change
repeats the reason for the change
questions.explanation: "However" introduces a contrast: the doors open earlier, but the office does not, so the change has a limit.

questions.stem: The letter is written mainly for:
questions.explanation: It opens "Dear Families" and refers to work schedules and reporting absences, which are concerns of students' families.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages disagree mainly about whether young students should:
options: do short math or spelling drills at home
be given any homework that takes an hour
questions.explanation: Passage A would limit homework to reading; Passage B supports a few minutes of math facts or spelling practice. Neither defends hour-long homework.

questions.stem: With which statement would both authors most likely agree?
options: Young children should get no homework at all
Long homework assignments are a mistake
questions.explanation: Passage A says long assignments teach children to dislike school; Passage B says to keep assignments short, "not a burden." Both oppose long assignments.

questions.stem: Which statement best restates the main point of Passage A?
options: Reading at home helps more than drills
Worksheets teach math better than books
Children should read alone each night
Homework should be longer in second grade
questions.explanation: Passage A says twenty minutes with a book does more good than an hour of drills and that homework should be reading with a family member, not reading alone.

questions.stem:
Read the sentences from a district report:

(1) The district opened two new elementary schools in 2024. (2) Each school has room for about 600 students. (3) The new buildings are the most attractive in the county. (4) Both schools have a library and a gym.

Which sentence states an opinion rather than a fact?
questions.explanation: "The most attractive in the county" is a judgment that cannot be checked. The opening date, capacity and facilities can all be verified.

questions.stem:
"Our school should switch to tablets instead of printed textbooks. Tablets will save money, because printed textbooks must be replaced every few years."

Which statement, if true, most weakens this argument?
options: Tablets can hold several books at once
Tablets must also be replaced every few years
Printed textbooks weigh far more than tablets
questions.explanation: The argument rests on tablets avoiding the cost of regular replacement. If tablets also need replacing just as often, that cost saving disappears.

questions.stem:
"After the third fire drill in one week, the students were running out of steam."

As used here, "running out of steam" means:
questions.explanation: The expression is colloquial for becoming tired or losing enthusiasm; it has nothing literal to do with heat or steam.

questions.stem: The prefix "pre-" means before, and the root "dict" means to say or speak. Using these clues, a "prediction" is:
options: a statement made before an event
a reason given after an event happens
a rule that must be followed
questions.explanation: Before plus say gives something said before it happens, which is what a prediction is.

questions.stem: A teacher wants ideas for using the garden to teach measurement. Which chapter should she read first?
questions.explanation: Chapter 6, "Lessons in the Garden: Science and Math," is about teaching with the garden, and measurement is math.

questions.stem: On which pages would a reader most likely find advice on finding a sunny spot for the garden?
questions.explanation: Chapter 2, "Choosing a Site: Sun, Water and Access," begins on page 9, and Chapter 3 begins on page 21, so the chapter runs from page 9 to 20.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: Total visits fell from March to April
The computer lab was busiest in January of all months
Children's room visits rose sharply in April
questions.explanation: Children's room visits climbed from 940 to 1,210 in April. Lab visits peaked in March, adult visits fell in February and April, and the April total (2,920) is higher than March's (2,730).

questions.stem: In which month did the children's room have more visits than the adult reading room?
questions.explanation: Only in April (1,210 to 1,020) did the children's room lead. In every other month adult visits were higher.

questions.stem: A bulletin board is 6 feet long. How many inches long is it?
questions.explanation: There are 12 inches in a foot, so 6 × 12 = 72 inches. 60 comes from using 10 inches per foot.

questions.stem: A rectangular school garden is 12 feet long and 8 feet wide. How many feet of fencing are needed to go all the way around it?
questions.explanation: Perimeter = 2 × (12 + 8) = 40 feet. 20 counts only one length and one width, and 28 leaves out one length.

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate of 398 × 21?
questions.explanation: Round to 400 × 20 = 8,000. The exact product, 8,358, is close to that.

questions.stem: A teacher has 28 essays to grade and expects each to take about 5 minutes. If she starts at 3:30 p.m. and works without a break, about when will she finish?
questions.explanation: 28 × 5 = 140 minutes, which is 2 hours 20 minutes. 3:30 p.m. plus 2 hours 20 minutes is 5:50 p.m.

questions.stem: A student's scores on five quizzes were 78, 85, 92, 81 and 89. What was her average score?
questions.explanation: The scores add to 425, and 425 ÷ 5 = 85.

questions.stem: On a standardized test reported in stanines (1 to 9), a student earned a stanine of 5. What does this score mean?
options: Her score was well above average
questions.explanation: Stanines divide scores into nine bands with 5 in the middle, so 5 is average. Stanines 7 to 9 are above average, and a stanine is not a percentile or a count.

questions.stem: A student's reading score is at the 70th percentile. Which statement is true?
options: He answered 70% of the questions correctly
He earned a score of 70 points
He beat about 70% of the group
He ranked 70th out of all test takers
questions.explanation: A percentile rank compares a score with a group: the 70th percentile means the score is higher than about 70% of the comparison group's scores. It says nothing about percent correct.

questions.stem: A box holds 4 red, 6 blue and 10 green markers. If one marker is taken without looking, what is the probability that it is blue?
questions.explanation: There are 4 + 6 + 10 = 20 markers and 6 are blue, so the probability is 6/20 = 3/10. 3/5 compares blue with green only.

questions.stem: What is 1,248 ÷ 24?
questions.explanation: 24 × 50 = 1,200, and the remaining 48 is 24 × 2, so the quotient is 52.

questions.stem: What is -7 + 12 - 9?
What is 3/4 + 2/3?
questions.explanation: Use the common denominator 12: 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12. Adding tops and bottoms to get 5/7 is the common mistake.

questions.stem: What is 0.6 × 0.4?
questions.explanation: 6 × 4 = 24, and the factors have two decimal places in all, so the product is 0.24.

questions.stem: A school orders 24 notebooks at \$1.25 each and 3 boxes of pencils at \$4.50 per box. What is the total cost of the order?
If 3x + 7 = 31, what is x?
questions.explanation: Subtract 7 from both sides: 3x = 24. Divide by 3: x = 8. 24 is the value of 3x, not x.

questions.stem: Maria bought 3 packs of paper for a total of \$18 and some folders. What more must you know to find how much she spent in all?
options: The price of one pack of paper
The total cost of the folders
The number of folders she bought
The number of sheets in each pack
questions.explanation: The paper cost \$18 in all; only the folders' cost is missing. Knowing how many folders she bought is not enough without their price.

questions.stem: Which of the following also gives 25% of 48?
questions.explanation: 25% is one fourth, so 25% of 48 equals 48 ÷ 4 = 12.

questions.stem: What is 15% of 80?
questions.explanation: 15% of 80 = 0.15 × 80 = 12. Another way: 10% is 8 and 5% is 4, and 8 + 4 = 12. 120 misplaces the decimal point.

questions.stem: A school's enrollment grew from 400 students to 460 students. By what percent did enrollment increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is 60 students, and 60 ÷ 400 = 0.15, or 15%. Dividing by the new total (60 ÷ 460, about 13%) uses the wrong base.

questions.stem: Which number is between 1/4 and 1/2?
questions.explanation: 1/4 = 2/8 and 1/2 = 4/8, so 3/8 lies between them. 1/5 and 2/9 are less than 1/4, and 5/8 is more than 1/2.

questions.stem: Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: On a number line -7 is to the left of -4, so -7 is less than -4. Each of the others reverses the true order.

questions.stem: Which fraction is equal to 0.35?
questions.explanation: 0.35 = 35/100, which simplifies to 7/20. 35/10 is 3.5.

questions.stem: What is 4,682 rounded to the nearest hundred?
questions.explanation: The tens digit is 8, which is 5 or more, so round the hundreds up: 4,700.

questions.stem: All students in Room 12 passed the quiz. Jamal did not pass the quiz. Which statement must be true?
options: No one else failed the quiz
questions.explanation: If Jamal were in Room 12 he would have passed, so he cannot be in Room 12. The statements say nothing about other students outside the room.

questions.stem:
A supply order is shown below.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Studying the night before a test is always useless
Study spread over several days is remembered better
Cramming works for history but not math
Students learn most when lessons feel easy
questions.explanation: The passage presents research that spaced study improves later recall and ends by saying the night before should be the last of several sessions. It says outright that a final review is not useless.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does a little forgetting help memory?
options: Students study more after they forget
Forgetting makes room for new facts
Recalling a fading topic takes effort
Short sessions are easier to schedule
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says returning after a gap forces the student to work to bring the topic back, and that effort strengthens the memory.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, "familiar" is contrasted with:
options: being able to study for a long time without breaks
being able to recall something later
questions.explanation: The paragraph says feeling familiar with something "is not the same as being able to recall it a week later."

questions.stem: According to the passage, students who space their study often misjudge:
options: how long a test will take
how many topics they must cover
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says spacing feels harder, so these students believe, wrongly, that they are learning less.

questions.stem: A reader wants to test the claim that spacing works "even" for motor skills. Which evidence would be most useful?
options: A list of words students found hard
Results of a typing study using spaced practice
A survey of students' favorite times of day to study
questions.explanation: Typing is a motor skill, so a study comparing spaced and massed typing practice would directly test the claim. The other choices say nothing about motor skills.

questions.stem: The author mentions homework and quizzes in the fourth paragraph mainly to:
options: explain why students often dislike their homework
show that cramming is still common
suggest how teachers can build in spacing
argue that quizzes should be graded
questions.explanation: The sentence says teachers can build review into homework and quizzes "so that spacing happens without anyone having to choose it."

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did the dry soil blow away?
options: Its grasses had been plowed up
questions.explanation: The passage says that with the deep-rooted grasses gone, nothing held the dry soil in place when the winds came.

questions.stem: Which outline best fits the order of ideas in the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage moves from plowing in the 1920s, to the drought of the early 1930s, to the dust clouds, to the government's response in 1935.

questions.stem: Which detail from the passage best supports the idea that the dust storms were very large?
questions.explanation: Dust that traveled across the country to the Atlantic coast shows how big the storms were. The other details concern prices, methods and migration.

questions.stem: The government's plan described in the last sentence assumes that windbreaks and curved plowing would:
options: help keep soil from blowing away
bring more rain to the plains
questions.explanation: Both methods were adopted in response to soil blowing away, so the plan assumes they would slow wind and hold soil.

questions.stem: According to the notice, what will crews do right after marking existing pipes and lines?
questions.explanation: The notice lists the steps in order: mark the lines, then dig a trench and install the main, then connect homes and repave.

questions.stem: How much warning will a resident receive before water service is shut off?
questions.explanation: The notice says residents will receive a door notice at least 48 hours before service is interrupted. Four hours is the length of the shutoff.

questions.stem: Which conclusion can be drawn from the notice?
options: Parking is banned on all of Maple Avenue all summer
The finish date could change with weather
Every home will lose water for a day
The work will be done one home at a time
questions.explanation: The project is "expected to be finished by the end of August, weather permitting," so bad weather could delay it. Shutoffs are up to four hours, and parking is closed only on the block being worked.

questions.stem: Which reader would find the notice most useful?
options: A family living on Maple Avenue
questions.explanation: The notice tells residents when their water will be off and where they cannot park, information meant for people who live on the street.

questions.stem: How does the author of Passage B respond to the claim in Passage A?
options: By agreeing that students forget less
By saying summer break should be made longer
By noting the gains are small and uneven
questions.explanation: Passage A says shorter breaks mean less forgetting; Passage B answers that studies show only small, inconsistent differences in achievement.

questions.stem: Which information would be most relevant to settling the disagreement between the two passages?
options: Test scores before and after a district switched calendars
How families plan their summer vacations
The cost of running summer camps in each district
The number of holidays in each kind of calendar
questions.explanation: The authors disagree about whether year-round calendars improve learning. Achievement data from a district that changed calendars bears directly on that question.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes Passage B?
options: Results are mixed; schedules can clash
Most families prefer year-round school calendars
Long breaks cause students to forget
questions.explanation: Passage B says achievement differences are small and inconsistent and that siblings' vacations may not line up.

questions.stem:
"Every successful parent in our town has already signed up for the reading challenge. Don't be the one family left out!"

Which persuasive technique does this statement mainly use?
options: A comparison of costs and benefits
An appeal to fit in with others
questions.explanation: The statement pressures readers by claiming everyone else has joined and warning against being left out. It offers no data, costs or expert.

questions.stem:
A school newsletter for families contains this sentence: "Folks who can't be bothered to sign the permission slip will have kids stuck in the library during the trip."

Why is the tone of this sentence inappropriate for its audience?
options: It uses too many technical terms
It is too formal for a newsletter
It gives no date for the trip
questions.explanation: "Can't be bothered" and "stuck" sound scornful in a message meant to inform families politely. The problem is tone, not formality or jargon.

questions.stem:
"The new principal's first month was a whirlwind of meetings, visits and phone calls."

The word "whirlwind" suggests that the month was:
questions.explanation: A whirlwind spins quickly; the metaphor describes a rush of activity, not bad weather or conflict.

questions.stem:
"The coach asked the team to table the discussion until after the game."

In this sentence, "table" means:
questions.explanation: To table a discussion is to set it aside for later; the phrase "until after the game" confirms the meaning.

questions.stem: On which page would a reader look for how to get rid of used batteries safely?
questions.explanation: The index lists "Batteries, 44-47; safe disposal of, 47."

questions.stem: A student reads about clouds on pages 112 to 115 and wants related material. According to the index, where else should she look?
questions.explanation: The cloud entry says "See also Weather," which points to pages 116 to 121.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the survey?
options: Most eighth graders ride a bicycle
Bus riders are fewest in Grade 6
Car travel rises from Grade 6 to Grade 8
questions.explanation: Walkers rise from 40 to 52 to 61. Bus riders are most numerous in Grade 6, and car travel falls across the grades.

questions.stem: In Grade 8, which way of travel is the most common?
questions.explanation: In Grade 8, 72 students ride the bus, more than the 61 who walk, 57 in cars and 30 on bicycles.

questions.stem: How many quarts are in 3 gallons?
questions.explanation: There are 4 quarts in a gallon, so 3 × 4 = 12 quarts. 6 uses 2 quarts per gallon, which is the number of pints in a quart.

questions.stem: A package weighs 2 pounds 4 ounces. How many ounces is that?
questions.explanation: There are 16 ounces in a pound: 2 × 16 + 4 = 36 ounces. 24 comes from using 10 ounces per pound.

questions.stem: Which is the most reasonable temperature for a hot summer afternoon?
questions.explanation: Water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit and boils at 212, so 35 is near freezing, 55 is cool, and 95 is hot.

questions.stem: A square classroom is 14 feet on each side. How many feet of border trim are needed to go around the whole room?
questions.explanation: A square has four equal sides: 4 × 14 = 56 feet. 28 counts only two sides, and 18 adds 14 + 4.

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate of 49 × 31?
questions.explanation: Round to 50 × 30 = 1,500. The exact product is 1,519.

questions.stem: A student scored 82, 90, 76 and 88 on four tests. What score does she need on the fifth test to have an average of 85?
questions.explanation: An average of 85 on five tests needs a total of 5 × 85 = 425. Her four scores add to 336, so she needs 425 - 336 = 89.

questions.stem: In a class of 28 students, the ratio of boys to girls is 3 to 4. How many girls are in the class?
questions.explanation: The ratio has 3 + 4 = 7 parts, so each part is 28 ÷ 7 = 4 students. Girls are 4 parts: 4 × 4 = 16. 12 is the number of boys.

questions.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sections. Three of them are red. What is the probability that a spin does NOT land on red?
questions.explanation: Five of the 8 sections are not red, so the probability is 5/8. 3/8 is the probability of landing on red.

questions.stem: What is 37 × 46?
The temperature at noon was 5 degrees. By midnight it had fallen 12 degrees. What was the temperature at midnight?
questions.explanation: 5 - 12 = -7. Falling 12 degrees from 5 passes 0 after 5 degrees and goes 7 more below zero.
Change to improper fractions: 5/2 × 4/3 = 20/6 = 3 1/3. Multiplying the whole numbers and fractions separately (2 × 1 + 1/2 × 1/3) gives the wrong 2 1/6.
Line up the decimal points: 12.50 - 3.75 = 8.75. 16.25 is the sum, not the difference.

questions.stem: A class of 32 students is going to a museum. Admission is \$6.50 per student, and the bus costs \$120 for the group. What is the total cost of the trip?
questions.explanation: 32 × \$6.50 = \$208 for admission, plus \$120 for the bus, is \$328.

questions.stem: If x ÷ 4 - 3 = 5, what is x?
questions.explanation: Add 3 to both sides: x ÷ 4 = 8. Multiply by 4: x = 32. 8 is the value of x ÷ 4.

questions.stem: Lee knows that one pack of pens costs \$3.60. What more does he need to know to find the price of one pen?
options: The total he will spend today
The number of packs on the shelf
The number of pens in a pack
The number of packs he will buy
questions.explanation: The price of one pen is the pack price divided by the number of pens in the pack. The number of packs he buys does not change the price of one pen.

questions.stem: Which is another correct way to find 6 × 49?
questions.explanation: 49 = 50 - 1, so 6 × 49 = 6 × 50 - 6 × 1 = 300 - 6 = 294. Subtracting only 1 forgets to multiply the 1 by 6.

questions.stem: A book that usually costs \$40 is on sale for 30% off. What is the sale price?
questions.explanation: 30% of \$40 is \$12, so the sale price is \$40 - \$12 = \$28. \$52 adds the discount instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: A library had 250 visitors on Monday and 200 on Tuesday. By what percent did the number of visitors decrease?
questions.explanation: The decrease is 50, and 50 ÷ 250 = 0.20, or 20%. Dividing by Tuesday's 200 gives the wrong 25%.

questions.stem: Which list is in order from least to greatest?
questions.explanation: As decimals, 1/2 = 0.5 and 2/3 is about 0.67, so the order is 0.45, 0.5, 0.6, 0.67.

questions.stem: Which symbol belongs in the blank to make 3/5 ___ 0.65 true?
questions.explanation: 3/5 = 0.60, and 0.60 is less than 0.65, so the symbol is <.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 4(x + 3)?
questions.explanation: Multiply each term inside the parentheses by 4: 4(x) + 4(3) = 4x + 12. Leaving the 3 unmultiplied gives 4x + 3.

questions.stem: What is 7.846 rounded to the nearest tenth?
questions.explanation: The tenths digit is 8 and the next digit is 4, which is less than 5, so 7.846 rounds down to 7.8.

questions.stem: "If it rains, the class will have recess in the gym." Today the class had recess outside, not in the gym. If the rule was followed, which must be true?
questions.explanation: Rain always leads to recess in the gym. Since recess was not in the gym, it cannot have rained. The statement gives no information about cleaning or length.

questions.stem:
The table shows how many students are in each grade at a small school.

| Grade | Students |
|---|---|
| 3 | 28 |
| 4 | 35 |
| 5 | ? |
| 6 | 31 |
| Total | 120 |

How many students are in Grade 5?
A bar graph shows the number of books a class read each month: January 12, February 18, March 15 and April 24. Between which two months did the number of books increase the most?
questions.explanation: January to February is up 6, February to March is down 3, and March to April is up 9, the largest increase between neighboring months.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why barn owls live in barns
How barn owls hunt in the dark
Why mice are active at night
questions.explanation: Each paragraph explains part of how the owl hunts without light: its hearing, its face, its ears and its quiet wings.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how does the owl judge how far below it a sound is?
options: Its wings are covered in soft feathers
Its eyes see well in dim light
Its ears are set at different heights
Its face is shaped like a beak
questions.explanation: Because the ears sit at slightly different heights, a sound reaches one ear first, and from that difference the owl judges direction and height.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between the owl's wing feathers and its hunting?
options: Soft feathers help it see at night
Comb-like edges help it carry prey
Stiff feathers make it fly faster
Quiet flight lets it surprise prey
questions.explanation: Muffled flight means the owl can hear its prey while flying and the prey cannot hear the owl coming.

questions.stem: The author mentions the earlier assumption about the owl's eyesight in order to:
options: set up the finding about hearing
prove that owls have weak eyes
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states the old belief, then reports experiments showing hearing does most of the work. The author even says the eyes are sensitive.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, an owl whose facial feathers were trimmed would most likely:
questions.explanation: The facial disk collects sound and funnels it to the ears, so losing it would make sounds harder to locate.

questions.stem: What is the author's main claim?
options: Keyboarding should not be taught at all
questions.explanation: The column calls dropping cursive "a shortsighted trade" and ends by urging boards to restore it. The author says every student needs to type.

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, the phrase "on the other hand" introduces:
questions.explanation: The sentence before says typing can be learned at almost any age; the phrase introduces cursive, which is rarely learned later.

questions.stem: Which statement does the author present as the view of people who disagree?
options: Adults seldom write by hand at work
Typing can be learned at any age
An hour a week is a small price
questions.explanation: The third paragraph begins "Supporters of keyboarding point out that adults seldom write by hand at work," which the author then answers.

questions.stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly persuades by:
options: citing research on handwriting and memory
implying that opponents do not care
questions.explanation: "Any school board that cares about its students will restore it" suggests that boards who disagree do not care, a loaded appeal rather than evidence.

questions.stem: Which fact, if true, would most weaken the author's argument about historical documents?
options: Many older letters were written in pencil
Typing classes are popular with students
questions.explanation: The author says students who cannot read cursive cannot read many archival documents. If typed transcriptions are widely available, that reason loses force.

questions.stem: The prefix "mis-" means wrongly or badly. A student who misreads a question has:
questions.explanation: Mis- plus read means to read wrongly; rereading would be re-.

questions.stem:
"Although the bus was late, the field trip began on time because the museum agreed to hold the group's tour slot."

Which statement best restates this sentence?
options: The museum held the slot, so the trip was on time
The trip was late because the museum was busy
The bus was on time, but the tour started very late
The group missed its tour because of the bus
questions.explanation: The sentence says the trip still started on time despite the late bus, because the museum held the slot.

questions.stem:
"Classroom pets can teach children responsibility. Students take turns feeding the class hamster, changing its water and cleaning its cage."

What is the relationship between the two sentences?
options: The second gives examples of the first
The first explains why the second happens
questions.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim about responsibility; the second lists specific tasks that show it.

questions.stem:
A sign in a school hallway reads: "Students must not run in the hall without a pass."

Why could this sign be read in two ways?
options: It uses the word pass too often
It does not say who wrote the rule
It could ban all running or only some
It does not say which hall is meant
questions.explanation: It could mean running is allowed only for students who have a pass, or that no one may run at all and students in the hall need a pass. One reading bans only some running; the other bans all of it.

questions.stem: Which statement about the city's new park is an opinion?
options: It opened to the public in May
It has two playgrounds and a duck pond
It is the best spot in town for a picnic
questions.explanation: "The best spot in town for a picnic" is a judgment. The opening month, size and features can be checked.

questions.stem:
"(1) The school day at Hillcrest runs from 8:20 to 2:50. (2) That schedule leaves far too little time for recess. (3) Recess lasts 20 minutes. (4) Lunch lasts 30 minutes."

Which sentence expresses the writer's opinion?
questions.explanation: "Far too little time" is a judgment about the schedule. The times and lengths can all be verified.

questions.stem:
"Students who eat breakfast at school will do better on morning tests, so the district should expand its breakfast program."

This argument assumes that:
options: more students will eat if it grows
morning tests are harder than others
questions.explanation: Expanding the program helps test scores only if more students actually eat breakfast because of it. Cost and lunch preferences are not part of the reasoning.

questions.stem:
"Our library should stay open on Saturdays, because many working parents cannot visit during the week."

Which finding would most strengthen this argument?
options: Few staff members want to work weekend shifts
The library has a large collection of DVDs and games
Most Saturday visitors are parents who work on weekdays
The library first opened its doors in 1985
questions.explanation: If most Saturday visitors are parents who work on weekdays, that supports the claim that working parents rely on Saturday hours. Staffing preferences would weaken it.

questions.stem:
"Our team values every player equally. That is why only the top scorers are allowed to speak at the awards dinner."

What is the problem with this statement?
options: It does not name the team
questions.explanation: Claiming to value every player equally does not fit a rule that lets only top scorers speak; the second sentence undercuts the first.

questions.stem: A teacher needs to know how to record a student's absence. Which pages should she check?
questions.explanation: The index lists "Absences: ... recording, 15-16."

questions.stem: Under which entry would a reader find information about rubrics?
questions.explanation: Rubrics are listed under "Grading: ... rubrics, 38-40."

questions.stem: A teacher preparing for a parent conference that needs a Spanish interpreter should turn to page:
questions.explanation: The entry reads "Parent conferences, 50-55; ... with interpreters, 54."

questions.stem: The entry for substitutes says "See also Lesson plans." This means that:
options: the book has no pages on substitutes
related pages are under that entry
lesson plans are in a different book
questions.explanation: A "see also" note points to another index entry with related information; it does not give that entry's pages.

questions.stem: A reader wants to build a nest box. In which part should she look?
questions.explanation: Part Four is "Feeders, Baths and Nest Boxes."

questions.stem: A reader hears an unfamiliar call but cannot see the bird. Which pages are most likely to help?
questions.explanation: Part Three, "Identifying Birds by Song," starts on page 42 and Part Four starts on page 60.

questions.stem: How is the main body of the book organized?
options: From the rarest birds to the most common
From watching birds to recording them
By the region where birds live
From summer birds to winter birds
questions.explanation: The parts move from how to watch, to identifying, to attracting birds, through the seasons, to keeping a journal.

questions.stem: Where would a reader most likely find a list to check off species she has seen?
questions.explanation: The appendix is a "Checklist of 120 Common Species."

questions.stem: According to the table, which use accounts for the largest share of water?
questions.explanation: The toilet uses 33 gallons a day, 24% of the total, more than any other use.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: Leaks waste about an eighth of use
The household uses about 100 gallons a day
Faucets use the least water of any use
Showers use more water than toilets
questions.explanation: Leaks are 12% of use, about one eighth. Showers use less than toilets, "Other" is the smallest, and the total is 137 gallons.

questions.stem: Showers and faucets together account for about what share of daily use?
questions.explanation: 20% for showers plus 19% for faucets is 39%.

questions.stem: Which question can NOT be answered from the table?
options: What share of use the washer takes
Which use is the second largest
How much water leaks waste each day
questions.explanation: The table gives gallons and shares by use but nothing about the number of people. Leaks (17 gallons), the second largest use (shower) and the washer's share (16%) are all listed.

questions.stem: In which year was full-time enrollment lowest?
questions.explanation: Full-time enrollment fell to 3,900 in 2022, its lowest point, then rose.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes part-time enrollment from 2020 to 2024?
questions.explanation: Part-time enrollment went 5,100, 5,600, 6,000, 6,300, 6,350, an increase each year. It dipped only in 2025.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: Total enrollment fell every single year
questions.explanation: In every year the part-time figure is higher than the full-time figure. Full-time enrollment dipped through 2022, and the total grew overall.

questions.stem: By how many students did total enrollment change from 2020 to 2025?
How many feet are in 5 yards?
questions.explanation: There are 3 feet in a yard, so 5 × 3 = 15 feet. 60 is the number of inches in 5 feet.

questions.stem: A roll of paper is 90 inches long. How long is that in feet and inches?
questions.explanation: 90 ÷ 12 = 7 with 6 left over, so 90 inches is 7 feet 6 inches. Dividing by 10 gives the wrong 9 feet.

questions.stem: A gallon (128 fluid ounces) of juice is poured into 8-ounce cups. How many cups can be filled?
A triangle has sides of 9 inches, 12 inches and 15 inches. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: The perimeter is the sum of the sides: 9 + 12 + 15 = 36 inches.

questions.stem: A rectangular playground is enclosed by 130 yards of fence. The playground is 40 yards long. How many yards wide is it?
questions.explanation: Half the perimeter is one length plus one width: 130 ÷ 2 = 65, and 65 - 40 = 25 yards. 90 subtracts only one length from the whole perimeter, 65 is half the perimeter, and 50 subtracts both lengths but does not halve what is left.

questions.stem: A teacher has a 50-minute class period. She plans an 8-minute warm-up, a 25-minute lesson and 5 minutes to clean up. How many minutes are left for group work?
questions.explanation: 8 + 25 + 5 = 38 minutes are planned, and 50 - 38 = 12 minutes remain.

questions.stem: A test begins at 9:40 a.m. and lasts 1 hour 35 minutes. At what time does it end?
questions.explanation: 9:40 plus 1 hour is 10:40, and 35 more minutes is 11:15 a.m.

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate of 612 ÷ 29?
questions.explanation: Round to 600 ÷ 30 = 20. The exact quotient is a little over 21.

questions.stem: Six students scored 70, 85, 92, 78, 88 and 95 on a test. What is the median score?
questions.explanation: In order: 70, 78, 85, 88, 92, 95. The two middle scores are 85 and 88, and their mean is 86.5. About 84.7 is the mean, not the median.

questions.stem: Ana took a test with 200 other students, and her score was at the 60th percentile of that group. About how many of the 200 students scored below her?
questions.explanation: The 60th percentile means about 60% of the group scored below her: 0.60 × 200 = 120. About 80 scored at or above her, and 60 mistakes the percentile for a count of students.

questions.stem: Stanine scores run from 1 to 9. Which stanine shows below-average performance?
questions.explanation: Stanines 1 to 3 are below average, 4 to 6 average and 7 to 9 above average, so only 2 is below average.

questions.stem: In past years, about 1 in 5 students forgot to return a permission slip. If 35 students are given slips this year, about how many would you expect to forget?
questions.explanation: 1/5 of 35 is 7. 28 is the number expected to remember.

questions.stem: What is -15 - (-6)?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative is adding: -15 + 6 = -9. -21 comes from subtracting 6 instead of adding it.

questions.stem: What is 4/5 - 1/3?
questions.explanation: Use the common denominator 15: 12/15 - 5/15 = 7/15. Subtracting tops and bottoms gives the wrong 3/2.

questions.stem: What is 3.6 ÷ 0.12?
questions.explanation: Multiply both numbers by 100 to clear the decimal in the divisor: 360 ÷ 12 = 30.

questions.stem: 7 is what percent of 28?
questions.explanation: 7 ÷ 28 = 1/4 = 25%. 4 comes from dividing 28 by 7.

questions.stem: An order lists 15 rulers at \$0.80 each, 8 pairs of scissors at \$2.25 each and 2 staplers at \$6.40 each. What is the order total?
questions.explanation: Rulers \$12.00, scissors \$18.00, staplers \$12.80: \$12.00 + \$18.00 + \$12.80 = \$42.80. Adding the three unit prices gives \$9.45.

questions.stem: If 5x - 4 = 2x + 11, what is x?
questions.explanation: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x - 4 = 11. Add 4: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.

questions.stem: If 0.5n = 14, what is n?
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by 0.5, which is the same as multiplying by 2: n = 28. 7 comes from multiplying by 0.5 instead.

questions.stem: A bus leaves school at 7:15 a.m. and makes 8 stops on its route. What more must you know to find when it reaches the last stop?
options: Which driver is on the route
How long the whole route takes
How many seats the bus has
How many students ride the bus
questions.explanation: Arrival time is the start time plus the travel time. The number of stops is already given, and riders, seats and the driver do not tell how long the trip takes.

questions.stem: Dividing a number by 0.5 gives the same result as:
questions.explanation: 0.5 is 1/2, and dividing by 1/2 is the same as multiplying by 2. For example, 8 ÷ 0.5 = 16.

questions.stem: A school is sending 255 students on a trip. Each bus holds 52 students. How many buses are needed?
questions.explanation: 255 ÷ 52 is about 4.9. Four buses hold only 208 students, so a fifth bus is needed for the rest.

questions.stem: The price of a calculator rose from \$80 to \$100. By what percent did the price increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is \$20, and 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25, or 25%. Dividing by the new price gives the wrong 20%.

questions.stem:
A class tracked the number of books read each week.

| Week | Books read |
|---|---|
| 1 | 14 |
| 2 | ? |
| 3 | 19 |
| 4 | 22 |
| Total | 73 |

How many books were read in Week 2?
Which fraction is the greatest?
questions.explanation: As decimals: 5/6 is about 0.83, 4/5 = 0.8, 7/9 is about 0.78 and 3/4 = 0.75.

questions.stem: Which number lies between -3 and -2 on a number line?
questions.explanation: -2.5 is halfway between -3 and -2. -3.5 is less than -3, and -1.5 is greater than -2.

questions.stem: Which comparison is true?
questions.explanation: 0.1 = 0.10, which is greater than 0.07. -5 is less than -2, 1/3 is 0.333..., and 0.40 equals 0.4.

questions.stem: Which percent is equal to 1/8?
questions.explanation: 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125, which is 12.5%. 0.125% forgets to multiply the decimal by 100, and 8% confuses the denominator with the percent.

questions.stem: Which expression has the same value as 3 × 15 + 3 × 5?
questions.explanation: Both products share the factor 3, so 3 × 15 + 3 × 5 = 3 × (15 + 5) = 3 × 20 = 60.

questions.stem: About 2,349 people attended a school fair. What is that number rounded to the nearest thousand?
questions.explanation: The hundreds digit is 3, which is less than 5, so round down to 2,000.

questions.stem: What is \$14.96 rounded to the nearest dollar?
questions.explanation: The cents are 96, which is more than 50, so round up to \$15.

questions.stem: Some teachers at Elm School coach a sport. All coaches at Elm School attend the fall meeting. Which statement must be true?
options: All teachers attend the fall meeting
No teachers attend the fall meeting
Every coach at Elm is a teacher
questions.explanation: The teachers who coach are coaches, and all coaches attend, so at least some teachers attend. Nothing says every teacher coaches or every coach teaches.

questions.stem: "Students may join the robotics club if they are in grade 7 or they have a teacher's note." Which student may NOT join?
options: A grade 7 student with a note
A grade 6 student with a note
A grade 7 student with no note
A grade 6 student with no note
questions.explanation: With "or," meeting either condition is enough. Only a student who meets neither, not in grade 7 and without a note, is left out.

questions.stem: A circle graph shows the favorite subjects of 200 students: math 30%, reading 25%, science 20%, art 15% and other 10%. How many more students chose math than art?
questions.explanation: Math: 30% of 200 = 60. Art: 15% of 200 = 30. The difference is 60 - 30 = 30 students. 90 is the two subjects added together.
